extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers of science concerned with methods of experimental causal inference
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and conceptual rules for discovering causal relations by observation and experiment: the canonical methods (Difference, Agreement, Joint/Indirect, Residues, and Concomitant Variations), their canons, examples, limitations, and required precautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference (requirements for direct causal proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare two instances (A B C and B C) which are alike in every circumstance except the presence/absence of A; if a occurs in the one with A and not in the one without A, A is the cause (or part of the cause) of a. The method requires instances differing only in the one antecedent and therefore yields certainty of causation when its requisitions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer artificial experiments because an experiment typically introduces a single, definite change into a well-known pre-existing state of things, making it feasible to satisfy the Method of Difference. Ensure the pre-existing state and the produced state differ in nothing except the tested antecedent. Beware: the observed effect might be produced not by the antecedent itself but by the means used to produce the antecedent; test this possibility by additional experiments. When the method's requisitions cannot be met (e.g., in spontaneous natural phenomena with many uncontrolled variables), the Method of Difference is commonly impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine any instances in which a phenomenon occurs; if all such instances agree in some circumstance A, then A is an invariable antecedent (or a is an invariable consequent of A). This method establishes uniformities (laws of phenomena) but does not by itself determine causal direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when artificial experimentation is impossible or when instances of the phenomenon can be gathered observationally. The Method of Agreement often suggests which antecedent to test by the Method of Difference. It yields evidence of connection but generally cannot by itself prove causation or direction of causation; to decide cause vs. effect one must be able to produce the one by means of the other (i.e., apply the Method of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference) — THIRD CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while two or more instances in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance, the circumstance in which alone the two sets of instances differ, is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a double employment of the Method of Agreement: show (a) instances where a occurs all contain A, and (b) instances where a does not occur all lack A. The two independent agreements corroborate each other and approximate a Difference proof. Limitations: it is not as cogent as a direct Method of Difference because one can rarely be sure that the affirmative instances agree only in A or the negative only in not-A; still, it is a powerful improvement over simple agreement and useful when direct Difference is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues — FOURTH CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from any phenomenon such part as is known by previous inductions to be the effect of certain antecedents; the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats the total phenomenon as the sum of known effects plus a residual effect attributable to overlooked antecedents. This method is a modification of the Method of Difference: the 'negative' instance is arrived at deductively (by subtracting known effects) rather than observed. The residue gives a hypothesis about the cause C of the remaining effect c, but this evidence is not complete unless (a) the prior inductions that assigned effects to other antecedents were reliable (preferably obtained by Difference), and (b) C can be produced separately or its agency can be accounted for by deduction from known laws. The Method of Residues is especially fertile for discovering obscure or overlooked causes but must be followed by specific tests when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations — FIFTH CANON
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected with it through some fact of causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when one phenomenon's variations (in quantity, direction, position, etc.) are found to be invariably accompanied by variations in another. Precautions: concomitance alone does not decide cause vs. effect because both may be effects of a common cause; attempt to produce the one by means of the other (Difference) if possible. For reliable inference, retain other antecedents unchanged while varying the candidate cause; the concomitance itself should be established by the Method of Difference when feasible. When numerical relations are observed (e.g., doubling A doubles a), knowledge of absolute quantities permits stronger inferences about the extent to which a is due to A. Beware extrapolating numerical laws beyond the limits of observed variation because different laws may produce similar behavior in narrow ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and role of artificial experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: An experiment, by introducing a perfectly definite change into a well-known pre-existing state of circumstances, commonly produces the pair of instances required by the Method of Difference and thus facilitates direct causal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a previous state of things with which you are well acquainted so no unforeseen alteration is likely to pass unobserved; introduce the phenomenon rapidly so other elements do not change. Artificial experiments are especially valuable for phenomena we can modify or control, since they help satisfy the strict requisitions of direct induction. Nonetheless, check that the effect is not produced by the means of producing the change (control for experimental artifacts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions, common precautions, and limitations for all methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Several recurring requirements and cautions permeate the methods: ability to isolate antecedents, certainty that instances agree or differ only in specified respects, control of other antecedents during variation, knowledge of absolute quantities when inferring numerical laws, and awareness that observational ranges may mislead extrapolation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always endeavor to keep other antecedents unchanged while testing one variable; recognize when antecedents are inseparably combined (then Agreement or Concomitant Variations may be the only resources); verify that observed concomitance is not due to a common hidden cause; when using numerical concomitance, ascertain absolute quantities to identify the true functional relation and avoid mistaking one law for another in narrow ranges. Accept that some permanent causes cannot be removed but may be modified (quantity or position) and that such modifications can provide evidence of causal connection. Where possible, follow inductive suggestions with direct experimental tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the four methods and epistemic status
rubrics_metrics.description: The four methods (Difference, Agreement, Residues, Concomitant Variations) are claimed to be the only possible modes of direct experimental (a posteriori) inquiry for ascertaining laws of succession of phenomena; some (e.g., Residues) require auxiliary deduction and have conditional certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat conclusions from these methods according to their method-specific strengths: Method of Difference yields the strongest direct proof of causation when its strict conditions are met; Agreement yields laws/uniformities but weaker causal claims; Residues and Concomitant Variations are powerful but carry particular uncertainties (dependence on prior inductions, limits of extrapolation, potential hidden causes). Use deduction to supplement and test inductive inferences where appropriate.
